label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
# Glenmore

I want to tell you all something properly, in one place, and I'm sorry that some of you have already heard pieces of it from someone else. That was my doing. I should have rung the people who needed to hear it first, and I didn't. Some of you found out on a WhatsApp message, and that's not how any of you should have heard news about your grandfather's house.

So here it is, all of it, as plainly as I can put it.

The house at Glenmore, the old Mulkerrin place out past Oughterard, is sold. The sale was agreed on 3 November, and it closes on 15 January 2027. The buyers are Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, so some of you will know the family name. They have two small children and they want to live in the house. They are not buying it to rent out for holidays or to put a sign on the gate. They want a home there.

Some of you will be thinking that I'm letting go of Tom's place too quickly. I've thought that too. I'd like you to understand why I did it anyway.

## The house

Pádraig Mulkerrin built Glenmore in 1931. He was Tom's grandfather, and he put the house up with his own hands and a few men from the parish, out of stone from the top field. Tom was born there. He grew up there with his brothers, in the back kitchen with the range that never drew properly unless you talked to it. His mother died in the front bedroom. When we were young and had no money, we drove out from Galway on a Sunday and Tom would walk the whole boundary with the dog, pointing out where the old well was and where the cattle used to get through the wall.

The lake is below the house, at the bottom of the rough field. Most of you have been in it, or your parents have. Declan refused to come out of it one summer until his lips were blue, and I had to bring a towel down to the edge and stand there shouting at him. The children were all taught to swim in that water. It's cold and it's brown and it's the best thing about the place.

It was also where Tom proposed to me, in 1979. We were in the haggard behind the house, in the rain, and the cattle were watching us from the other side of the gate like they were waiting for the answer as well. I said yes before he had finished the sentence. He never let me forget that I hadn't let him finish.

## Why I'm selling

Tom died in March 2024. I've been driving out to Glenmore every second Saturday since then, which is about forty minutes each way from here. I open the windows, run the taps, light a fire in the front room so the damp doesn't get into the good furniture, and check the pipes and the water tank. I tell myself I'm looking after the house for him. Most of the time I'm just sitting in the kitchen with a cup of tea and not wanting to leave.

That's the honest picture, and I know it's not the whole of it.

The house needs more money than I have. In September we had Ó Flaithearta out to do a survey. The slates need doing, and the back chimney is in a bad way. The quote for the roof work is €38,000. There's also damp coming through the back bedroom wall that nobody has been able to fix properly. And the septic tank has to be replaced before anyone can sell the place to anyone, so that was going to come out of my pocket regardless. I did the sums more times than I can count. I could have borrowed against the house in Galway, or asked some of you for help, or started letting the land. I thought about all of them. None of them would have fixed the thing underneath, which is that I'm seventy-one, I live alone in Galway, and I can't keep Glenmore going on my own.

I also have to be honest about the fear. Since the autumn I have been frightened to be out there by myself. I'll say more about why below, because some of you need to know it.

When I had the first offer in the summer, from a group in Dublin, I didn't take it. That offer was higher. I took the lower one on purpose, from Aoife and Kevin. Partly it's a fair price, and I'm not ashamed of wanting a fair price. But mostly I wanted the house to go to a young family who would sleep in its bedrooms and cook in its kitchen and let the children go down to the lake in the summer. Tom always said the house should have children in it, not be a museum. I didn't want it turned into somewhere people came to take photographs and leave again. I wanted it lived in. I'm not sure I'd have had the strength to make that choice if Tom had been alive. I'm not sure it's the right choice for everyone. But it's the one I made, and I'm at peace with it, mostly.

## What I should have done differently

I should have told Declan first, and I didn't. I knew he would be upset, and I was putting off the conversation because I didn't want to have it. Then the news got out through Gráinne, and by the time I finally sat down to call Declan, he already knew the most important part and had heard it from someone else.

He rang me in the middle of his night. He was angry, and he said I was "selling Dad." I said some things back that I shouldn't have said. I won't repeat them here. I was short with him and I made it sound like he had no right to an opinion, when he had every right to one. I was hurt, and I took that hurt out on him, which I'm not proud of.

I also didn't think about how the rest of you would feel. Úna, you and Declan were both out at Glenmore for Tom's birthday last year, and I should have talked to you both before anything else was settled. Cousins in Boston, Perth and Leeds: you're far away, so you're not going to be able to come out to the house very often, and I know that. I should have given you the chance to say what the house means to you before the sale was agreed. I didn't, and I'm sorry.

I'm not writing this to apologise for the decision. I've thought about it for close to two years, and I'm not going to pretend it was an easy one. I am writing to say sorry for how you all found out. That part was wrong, and it's on me.

## What's being kept

Some of you will want to know what you're getting to keep, so here is the list.

Úna, the dresser is yours. It's the one from the back kitchen, the one with the chipped corner Tom always blamed on his brother Seán. It's going to your house in Galway this spring and it's going to stay in the family.

Pádraig's fiddle is coming to me, and it will go to whoever in the family wants it when I'm gone. It needs a new bridge and a good clean, and I'm going to have that done before anything else. Declan, I know you've always wanted to try to play it. I'll put it aside for you.

The photographs are all coming with me. There are boxes of them: Pádraig and his brothers outside the house in 1932, Tom at about six on the wall with the dog, your Granny Kathleen at the kitchen table at a wedding nobody can remember the name of, all of us in the haggard on the day Gráinne fell in the lake. I'm going to have every good one scanned and sent to everyone. That's a promise.

The Sacred Heart lamp is coming to Galway. It was lit in that front room every night of Tom's childhood. I'm not going to let it go to strangers.

The gate sign is coming too, the painted one with GLENMORE on it that Tom made when we were first married. The Joyces are kind people and they've said they'd like to keep the name. But the sign itself comes home with me, and I'll find a place for it.

Here's what I'm not keeping, and I'd like you to know it: the furniture, the old range, the beds, the boxes in the attic. Those are going in the clear-out in January. Some of it is going to a house sale, and some of it is going to the tip, and I'm not going to pretend that doesn't hurt. I've decided that if I try to keep everything, I'll lose the house and the house will lose me. What matters isn't the wardrobe. It's the people and the memories.

And the Joyces have agreed that family can come out and walk the land any time. I asked them. They said yes without any hesitation, and I was very touched by that. You can walk to the old well. You can go down to the lake. You can stand in the haggard. Aoife has said the children would love to meet their cousins from Perth and Boston and Leeds, if any of you are over.

## The fall

Last February I slipped on the step at the back door in the frost. I was out there on my own, carrying in the water and the bread. I went down hard and I couldn't get up. I lay on the cold concrete for about twenty minutes before I could get myself to my knees and drag myself up against the door. My hip was bruised for a month and my wrist still aches when the weather turns.

I didn't tell anybody. I didn't ring a single one of you. I drove home to Galway that evening and told myself I was fine, and I've told myself that every time I've been out there since. But I'm not fine. I'm not able to be out there on my own in the winter, and I don't think I should have to be. That's the other reason I'm selling. I wanted you to know, because you should have known, and because it's part of why I can't go on.

I'm not telling you this so you'll worry about me or drop everything to come and check on me. I'm telling you because I think I should have told you a year ago. Please ring me. Please ring me without waiting for a reason.

## What I've learned

Over the best part of two years, I have come to see that I can keep Tom's memory without keeping the house. I didn't believe that at first. I thought the house was the only place he still existed. But he's in the way Declan laughs, and the way Úna holds a cup, and the way the children pester you about the lake. He's in the photographs and in the fiddle and in the stories we'll all keep telling for the rest of our lives. Glenmore was where he came from. It isn't the only place he lives.

I'm not going to pretend I've made peace with all of it. I still have days where I can barely look at the front gate. But I have made a decision, and I'm going to live with it honestly and try to do right by all of you in the way I handle what comes after.

## The day out

On Sunday 13 December, before the house is cleared, I'd like us all to go out to Glenmore together. Come if you can. If you're in Galway or Mayo or Dublin, come for the day. If you're in Boston or Perth or Leeds and can't make it, we'll have the photographs sent to you and we'll talk on the phone that afternoon with the whole lot of us crowded round the speaker. There will be soup and sandwiches in the kitchen, and tea that tastes of the range, and a fire in the front room. Bring wellies. The haggard will be wet, and so will the lake walk.

Walk the boundary if you like. Go down to the lake, if anyone is brave enough to go in. Stand in the haggard for a while. Tell stories about Tom and Pádraig and Granny Kathleen, or don't, whatever you prefer. Take photographs. I'd like to see what you choose to take.

Anyone who wants to bring something to leave behind is welcome to do that as well. A plant for the garden, a note under the stone at the front step. The Joyces have said they'd be glad of it.

## To Declan

Declan, I know you're reading this, because you read everything I write. I know I hurt you, and I know you heard it from somebody else before you heard it from me. I'm sorry for that. I should have been the one to tell you, and I should have done it properly, sitting down with you, not ringing you at the end of a long day.

I'm not angry with you. I'm not angry about what you said on the phone either. You were grieving, and you were frightened for something that meant a lot to you. I understand that more than you might think.

The door is open. Whenever you're ready, I'd like to talk, properly, with no news to get in the way. Come out to Glenmore on the 13th if you can. You don't have to say anything. Just come and stand at the lake with me for a while, the way you used to, and we'll see what we have to say to each other after that.

I love you. I always have. I'll see you in December, I hope.

To everyone else: thank you for reading this far. I know it's a lot to take in at once, and I know some of you will have questions I haven't answered. Ask me. Ring me. I'll answer as honestly as I can.

With love from Galway,

reasons: It omits that Declan heard via Gráinne’s WhatsApp at 2 a.m. his time and does not explain why she will not wait until his summer visit.
